item.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Optimization for Compound AI
item.description:
Abstract

LLMs adapt to downstream tasks via RL (GRPO)
BUT language is a richer feedback (interpretable, flexible)
Enter GEPA: a prompt optimizer using NL rules—learned high-level rules by trial & error

Given:
- An AI system with ≥1 prompts
- Samples system-level trajectories (reasoning, tool calls, outputs)
- Reflects on them
- Diagnoses problems, proposes & tests prompt updates
- Combines complementary lessons from Pareto Frontier of its own runs

Findings:
- Few rollouts yield big gains
- Beats GRPO (+10% avg), MIPROv2 (+10%)
- Effective inference-time strategy for code/prompt optimization

Introduction

LLMs → multi-step agents + tool users
Fuzzy natural language + tool use (retrieval, code exec)
Goal: Optimize for downstream performance

Previous:
- RLVR/GRPO: Group Relative Policy Optimization
- Scalar reward per rollout, used for gradients
- Needs tens of thousands of rollouts
- Expensive (tool calls), budget-constrained

Key insight:
Rollouts = serialized language traces (instructions, reasoning, tool calls, errors).
Modern LLMs can understand these traces—so why use only scalar rewards?

  • Hypothesis: Algorithms that reflect & reason over these traces (in language) exploit language model priors more efficiently than classic RL.

GEPA: Genetic-Pareto Reflective Optimization

  • Reflective prompt optimizer for compound AI systems
  • NL feedback + evolutionary multi-objective search

Method:
1. Mutate every prompt using NL feedback
2. Accumulate high-level lessons from batch observations
3. Maintain Pareto front of candidates (avoids local optima)
4. Explore top-performing prompts per task instance

Benefits:
- Diversifies strategies → robust generalization
- Efficient: achieves gains with far fewer rollouts

Evaluation

Benchmarks:
- HotpotQA, IFBench, PUPA, HoVer
- Models: Open (Qwen3 8B), Proprietary (GPT-4.1 mini)

Results:
- GEPA > GRPO by up to 19%
- 35× fewer rollouts needed
- +10% avg improvement vs GRPO
- Beats MIPROv2 on every benchmark
- +14% aggregate gains (MIPROv2: +7%)

Practical:
- Single reflective update → large improvements
- Prompts not only numerically better—actually more interpretable/usable
- Works in budget-constrained/inference-time environments

Addressing Concern

  • “Isn’t GEPA just gaming metrics with weird prompts?”
    • Qualitative check: Prompts actually look and work better, not just metric-optimized
    • Sample-efficient, robust, generalizes well

Method: Key Steps

  1. Problem Statement
  2. GEPA Algorithm
    • 3.1 Genetic Optimization Loop
    • 3.2 Reflective Prompt Mutation
    • 3.3 Pareto-Based Candidate Selection
  3. Evaluation Setup (see paper for task/config details)

Summary

  • Leverages natural language for richer, more efficient optimization
  • Maintains diversity/Robustness: Pareto front avoids local minima
  • Beats strong RL baselines with fewer samples
  • Practical for real-world, resource-limited systems

item.title: MLE-STAR from Google
item.description:
Abstract

Agents can auto implement models via code generation.

But existing ways use: - Inherent knowledge - Coarse exploration strategies (modify code structure AT ONCE) - Limits ability to select task specific models - Limits deep exploration within specific components (deeper on feature engineering)

MLE-STAR: - External knowledge via search engine - Forms initial solution - Refines it by targeting specific components - Exploration from Ablation Studies - Novel ensembling method (suggested by MLE-STAR itself)

Results: MLE-bench Lite (kaggle comps) acc 64%

Introduction

MLE agents: (Guo et al., 2024; Hong et al., 2024; Jiang et al., 2025)

Evaluated on: MLE-bench’s Kaggle competitions (Chan et al., 2025)

Beats: - Jiang et al 2025 - AIDE - Guo et al. 2024 - DS Agent

1. The Core Idea

Search-assisted knowledge + Component-wise optimization + Smart ensembling

2. The Process Flow

Initial Code Generation

  • Creates first attempt at solution
  • Uses Google Search to look up modern, relevant ML techniques for that problem type

Identify Most Important Code Components

Code components: data preprocessing, feature engineering, model architecture, ensemble building

Ablation study approach: - “Turn off or replace one component at a time” - “See how much performance drops” - “The one that hurts performance most = most important”

Targeted Code Refinement

  • Picks most impactful component
  • Searches for ways to improve ONLY that part (not rewriting everything)

Improvement ideas from: - Past failed attempts (learning from mistakes) - Search results - New code generation

Repeat for Other Components

  • After improving one part → moves to another
  • Cycle continues until results stop improving significantly

Ensembling

Normal ensembling: Combining multiple trained models (voting, averaging, stacking)

MLE-STAR approach: - Generates multiple complete solutions - Designs its own ensemble method to merge them (not basic “majority vote”) - Tests and refines ensemble method iteratively

3. Why This Is Special

  • Search-assisted: Doesn’t rely only on built-in knowledge → actively pulls from internet
  • Component-wise optimization: Most systems try to improve everything at once; MLE-STAR focuses on parts that matter most
  • Smart ensembling: Custom combination methods vs “one model to rule them all”
  • Performance proof: More than doubled rate of top-medal finishes vs previous best baseline

4. Key Terms

  • Ensembling: Combining multiple models’ predictions to improve accuracy
  • Ablation study: Testing component importance by removing/altering it and measuring performance change
  • Feature engineering: Creating/transforming input features to help model learn better
  • Pipeline component: Modular part of ML workflow (preprocessing, model, post-processing)
  • Refinement: Iteratively improving specific code parts vs rewriting whole thing

Related Work

  • ReAct (Yao) - Reasoning + Action
  • HuggingGPT (Shen) - Multi-agent orchestration
  • Voyager - Minecraft exploration strategies
  • AlphaCode - Code generation
  • AutoML - Predefined search spaces need domain knowledge
  • MLAB (Huang) - ML automation
  • OpenHands (Wang) - Code agents
  • AIDE (Jiang) - Candidate solutions in tree structure
  • DS-Agent - Case-based reasoning for Kaggle

Need: Effective exploration strategies directly in Code Space

Results

64% accuracy on MLE-bench Lite Kaggle competitions

Beats existing baselines including AIDE and DS-Agent

More than doubled rate of top-medal finishes

item.title: Understanding Is a Poor Substitute for Convexity (Antifragility)
item.description:
Introduction: Missing the Asymmetry

Did you just get lucky or was it your aim?
Linear, teleological success stories fit physics.
In opaque, nonlinear fields (medicine, engineering), chance drives more breakthroughs.
Still, we build research programs around stories and direction—despite knowing better.

Key Point:
Chance alone can’t yield steady progress—unless the payoff function is asymmetric. Nonlinear payoffs let us systematically benefit from randomness.

  • Welcome uncertainty in the long run. It can hurt you less than it helps you.

Opaque Systems and Optionality

Trial and error + convexity = real progress
In experiments (cooking, science), keep what works, discard what doesn’t.
We have the option (not the obligation) to retain only favorable results.
This “optionality”—the ability to choose after the fact—lies behind convex research payoffs.

  • Optionality liberates us from inflexible roadmaps, predictions, and stories.
  • Some research results have abnormally large long-term impact (penicillin, black swans, GPT-5 scale events).

Analogy: Research vs. Financial Options

  • Research is like running many small, cheap experiments (like owning lots of “call options”).
  • Failures cost little; one big win changes everything.
  • In finance, option buyers pay a premium and the game is zero-sum.
  • In research, no one sells you upside or limits your payoff:
    • One discovery grows the overall pie of knowledge, not just shifting value between players.

Why Uncertainty Is Valuable

  • Which projects should be funded?
    • Mathematical Principle: In convex systems, both convexity (asymmetry of payoff) and volatility (randomness) work in your favor.
  • Gains > Harms if the payoff is asymmetric.

Convexity Bias (Jensen’s Inequality)

  • Suppose a coin:
    • Linear: win $1, lose $1. EV = $0.
    • Convex: win $10, lose $1. EV = +$4.5.
    • The more convex the scenario, the higher the built-in advantage.
  • Jensen’s inequality: Convex functions benefit from randomness.

Bottom Line:
- The more convex the payoff, and the more uncertain the environment, the greater the net expected gain.

Antifragility: Benefiting From Disorder

  • Fragile things dislike volatility (coffee cups).
  • Antifragile things love volatility (evolution, discovery).
  • Convexity bias (not mere luck) can be defined, measured, and used to guide research funding.

Seven Rules of Antifragile (Convex) Research

  1. Convexity > Knowledge
    • Improving the payoff shape (limiting downside, stretching up side) matters more than understanding the target deeply. Lower costs per attempt to maximize upside from uncertainty.
  2. 1/N Strategy for Convex Bets
    • Spread the budget widely: make N as large as possible, allocating 1/N to each experiment/project.
    • “Fat tails” mean rare events dominate long-term results—don’t put all your eggs in one basket, and don’t try to pick the winner in advance.
  3. Serial Optionality
    • Plans must allow frequent adjustments (“highways with many exits”).
    • Short, flexible investments vastly outperform rigid, long-term bets.
  4. Nonnarrative Research
    • Favor action and opportunistic agents over story-driven plans.
    • Track records come from those who keep switching until something works, not from those who guess the ending in advance.
  5. Practice → Theory
    • Major breakthroughs often follow from tinkering (convex practice) rather than top-down theory.
  6. Premium for Simplicity
    • The simplest technologies are easily missed; avoid needless complexity.
    • Simple, modular setups are more robust in uncertain, opaque environments.
  7. Catalog Negative Results (“Via Negativa”)
    • Knowing what doesn’t work is powerful. Fund, capture, and spread negative results to reduce wasted effort.

Is All This Just Lottery Thinking?

Critics say: “This sounds like buying lottery tickets.”
But key differences make research optionality superior:

  • You control your “ticket price” and can lower trial costs.
  • Upside in research can be unlimited; lotteries have capped payoffs.
  • You keep only winnings and cut losses via optionality.
  • Learning and adaptation can increase your odds over time (lotteries are static).
  • Diversification (many independent tries) raises expected value—unlike buying more lottery tickets.
  • Research creates positive-sum value (society wins); lotteries are zero-sum with a house edge.
  • Hits spawn new opportunities; lottery wins don’t.

Quick Math: - 100 research trials × $1 = $100 spent; if one scores $200 and rest fail, EV = +$101. - 100 lottery tickets × $1 = $100; average return $0.60 per ticket: EV = −$40.

To avoid “lottery-like” waste: - Keep trials cheap - Ensure upside is not capped - Avoid correlated bets - Learn as you go and cut losses fast

Appendix: Visual Intuitions

  1. Fat vs. thin tails: Rarer outcomes matter much more in fat-tailed systems.
  2. Right tail (lognormal): Small set of rare wins dominate value.
  3. Left tail (negative events): Most events harmless, but must cap rare disasters.
  4. Operations: Tails, not averages, dictate most real-life quality (e.g., user pain in computing).

Rule of thumb: Cap the left tail (risks), keep the right tail (potential).

References

Cites works by Jacob (1977), Bachelier (1900), Jensen (1906), Taleb & Douady (2013), Mokyr (2002), Kealey (1996), and others—see original text for full list.

item.title: Reflexion: Language Agents with Verbal Reinforcement Learning
item.description:
Abstract

Traditional RL:
- Requires extensive training samples
- Expensive fine-tuning

REFLEXION Approach:
- Reinforcement through linguistic (verbal) feedback instead of rewards only

Key Mechanism:
- Agents reflect verbally on task feedback
- Maintain memory buffer of reflective text
- Several reflection styles tested
- Improves performance baseline

Result:
- 91% pass@1 on HumanEval (code)
- Surpasses GPT (80%)
- Code and repo

Related Work

  • ReAct, SayCan, Toolformer, HuggingGPT, WebGPT
  • All: Actions learned in context
  • Problem: RL remains costly

Semantic Gradient Signal

  • Useful feedback = essential
  • Credit assignment = challenging
  • “Generating summary” = hard

Reflexion: Feedback Mechanisms

Three feedback sources:
1. Simple binary environmental feedback
2. Predefined heuristics
3. Self-evaluation (e.g., self-written unit tests in programming)

  • All signals are amplified into natural language summary
  • Summary stored in long-term memory buffer

Why Reflexion Helps

  • Captures nuanced feedback
  • Provides interpretable episodic memory
  • Lite: Little supervision needed

Drawbacks:
- Relies on self-eval quality
- No formal guarantee of success

Experiments

  • Decision-making, reasoning, programming tasks
  • Benchmarks:
    • AlfWorld: +22%
    • HotpotQA: +20%
    • HumanEval: +11%

Key achievement:
- pass@1 improvement:
- HumanEval: 91% (vs. GPT 80%)

Ablation + Analysis

  • Studies with different feedback signals
  • Examined methods of feedback incorporation
  • Compared agent types
  • Findings: Reflection/additional feedback directly impacts performance

Further Reading

  • Reflexion codebase and paper

10 key points exclusive

Caveat:

5 is for people who want the TLDR on picking config for TRL verifiers and Unsloth (not interested on coding things from scratch)

1. Simulating Tasks

to do RL we need tasks

Syllogism

Premise 1

Premise 2

Conclusion

Propositional Logic Task

Harder

Reasoning Gym

Reasoning Gym Library - Rewards (Telegraphic Summary)

Core Function:

reasoning_gym.create_dataset() → generates propositional logic examples

Makes prompt creation/validation easy

System Architecture:

LLM generates: <think>reasoning</think> <answer>result</answer>

Extract function: regex pulls answers from XML tags

Score function: +1 reward for correct, 0 for incorrect

Testing Flow:

Loop through dataset questions

Generate LLM response

Extract answer via regex

Score correctness

Results by Model:

Manual Input: ✅ Works correctly

GPT-4.1 Mini: ✅

  • Solid responses
  • Follows XML format
  • No additional training needed

SmallLM135M (135M params): ❌

  • Flawed reasoning
  • Ignores XML instruction format
  • Can’t extract answers → can’t score

Next: Reinforcement learning to improve small model performance

GRPO visually explained

Two Major Phases:

Experience Collection → LLM interacts, fills buffer

Training → Update model weights for better rewards

Experience Collection Phase

Step-by-Step:

Sample batch → e.g., 2 questions from environment

Tokenize + Generate → Multiple responses via high temperature sampling

Detokenize → Convert back to string responses

Score → Environment generates reward for each response

✅ Correct + proper format = high rewards

❌ Incorrect/wrong format = low rewards

Advantage Calculation:

Standardize rewards → zero mean, std dev = 1

Group Relative = relative advantage vs other responses to same question

Why called “Group Relative Policy Optimization”

Buffer Storage (4 components per experience):

Full sequence → system prompt + question + LLM answer

Response mask → binary indicator of LLM-generated tokens

Group relative advantage → standardized reward score

Log probabilities → of generated tokens (used in training phase)

Next: Training phase uses these stored experiences to update model weights

Policy Optimization & PPO Loss (Telegraphic)

Core Objective: Maximize Policy Gradient

Equation Breakdown:

First Σ → loops over G responses per question

Second Σ → loops over tokens (t=1 to length) in each response

Result: Nested loop through every token in batch

Key Components

π(θ) × A_it:

A_it = advantage of each token

The easiest way to assign advantage to each token is..

Simple version: Copy response advantage to all tokens

Logic: Every token equally responsible for correct answer

Example: +1 response advantage → +1 for each token

π term (Probability):

Probability of token t in response i

Given: question Q + previous tokens (autoregressive)

Training Logic

Fixed: Advantages (from environment rewards) Variable: Token probabilities (from LLM)

To maximize objective:

↑ Probability of tokens with positive advantage

↓ Probability of tokens with negative advantage

Advanced Components

Importance Sampling (π/π_old):

π_old = policy during experience collection

π = current training policy

Reweights advantages between old/new networks

Clipping Term:

Purpose: Regularization - prevents extreme weight updates

Constraint: Ratio clamped between (1-ε, 1+ε)

Effect: “Don’t change weights too quickly”

Result: Model learns to generate tokens → higher advantages → correct answers
